hints: Think about the broad group of pathogen involved - measles is not caused by a bacterium or fungus, so what type of infectious particle must it be?
walkthrough:
Recall the pathogen type**
Measles is a viral disease. It spreads very easily from person to person through droplets, which is typical of a highly infectious virus rather than a bacterium.

hints: Start by looking at the total height of the bars over time. Do the totals stay steady or go up and down, and is there one year that looks very different from the others?
Now compare the grey part and the white part of the bars. In most years which colour is larger, and when does this switch?
Pick out numbers to support your points - what is the highest total value and in which month and year, and are cases higher at the start or end of each yearly cycle?
walkthrough:
See the overall fluctuation**
The total height of each bar is the global total. It does not stay constant. It falls and rises repeatedly, giving about five outbreaks or peaks between Jan 2008 and Dec 2012.

Spot the 2010 anomaly**
2010 stands out clearly. The bars are much taller, reaching about 42 000 in June 2010, and the high numbers last for many months from Jan to Aug 2010, longer than the peaks in 2008, 2009, 2011 and 2012.

Add seasonal and regional detail**
Within each year, cases are higher in the first months (Jan-May) than later in the year. The white section (rest of world) is larger than the grey section (Africa) in every year except 2010, when Africa contributes most of the huge peak.

Final answer: Number of cases fluctuates with repeated outbreaks/peaks; much higher and longer-lasting epidemic in 2010 with highest peak of 42 000-43 000 cases; numbers higher at beginning of each year than at end; rest of world greater than Africa in every year except 2010.

hints: Start with what is in the vaccine. What foreign molecules are introduced and which cells first take them up and display them?
Think about how the body finds the very few lymphocytes that match. What does it mean for a B cell receptor to fit the antigen?
Once the matching cell is found, what must happen to its numbers before enough antibody can be made?
Link the final cell type to antibody production and consider which other lymphocyte helps to activate B cells.
walkthrough:
Antigen presentation starts the response**
The measles vaccine contains measles antigens. Phagocytes such as macrophages engulf them and present the antigen fragments on their surface to lymphocytes.

Clonal selection finds the match**
There are millions of different B-lymphocytes, each with a different antibody receptor. Only the B cell whose receptor has a complementary shape to the measles antigen will bind it. That is clonal selection.

Clonal expansion builds numbers**
That selected B cell is activated, helped by T helper cells which release cytokines. It then divides repeatedly by mitosis to form a large clone of identical cells. This takes time, which explains the 7-10 day delay.

Plasma cells make antibody**
Many cells of the clone differentiate into plasma cells. Plasma cells are protein-secreting factories that produce and release specific antibody into the blood, so antibody concentration then begins to rise.

Final answer: Vaccine antigens are presented; specific B-lymphocyte selected by clonal selection; activated B-lymphocyte divides by mitosis in clonal expansion with T helper cell stimulation; B-lymphocytes develop into plasma cells which secrete antibody.

hints: Think about movement of people. Even if most people in a country are vaccinated, what happens if someone brings the virus in from outside?
Think about why protection in a population is never perfect - who might still be susceptible and why might the vaccine itself sometimes not work?
walkthrough:
New virus can be imported**
Measles is highly infectious. People who caught it abroad such as tourists, migrants or returning travellers can bring it into a vaccinated country and pass it to susceptible contacts.

The population is never 100% protected**
Herd immunity for measles needs over 90% immunity. Some people are not vaccinated because they are too young, refuse vaccination, live in remote or war zones, or miss boosters. Others do not respond due to weak immune systems or malnutrition, and reconstituted vaccine loses effectiveness if the cold chain is not maintained.

Final answer: Infection introduced by travellers from abroad; herd immunity not achieved as some unvaccinated, e.g. too young, refusal, remote areas, or no booster, or non-responders with weak immunity, or vaccine damaged by poor cold chain.
